The night sky has always felt like an invitation. On a clear evening, away from city lights, you can look up and see thousands of stars, each one a sun with its own possible worlds. Some of those points of light left their homes millions of years ago; the photons reaching your eyes tonight started their journey when dinosaurs still walked the Earth. That simple fact never stops being astonishing.

What I find even more remarkable is how much we have learned from those distant sparks. Spectroscopy lets us read the chemical fingerprints of stars we will never visit. We know which ones are rich in metals, which are dying, which might host planets in their habitable zones. We have mapped the cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the Big Bang, and watched galaxies collide in slow motion across billions of years. All of this from a small rocky planet orbiting an ordinary yellow star in an unremarkable spiral arm.

Curiosity is the engine. It is the same impulse that made early humans track the seasons by the stars, that sent Voyager into interstellar space with a golden record, that now drives us to build telescopes the size of football fields and send robots to Mars. Every answer raises new questions. What lies beyond the cosmic horizon? Are we alone? How did consciousness arise from matter?

I like to think that writing, talking, and wondering are all part of the same project: trying to understand our place in a universe that is vastly larger and older than we are, yet still somehow accessible to a curious mind. The sky does not care whether we look up, but we are better for doing so.

What do you see when you look up?
